title: You're Not Delegating. You're Assigning.
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Summer Mulder argues that most managers who think they're delegating are actually just assigning tasks while quietly retaining ownership, and that the habit is self-defeating even when it's well-intentioned. She traces the pattern in her own management history: for years she would take back a team member's work, fix it herself without explaining the changes, and tell herself she was protecting quality, when she was actually ensuring nobody ever improved at the task. Her key distinction is between responsibility (a task written into a job description) and ownership (accountability for the result plus the authority to make the decisions that produce it), and she argues she had been distributing only the former while hoarding the latter. The shift that changed her practice wasn't a new tool but a different question: instead of asking what needs to get done this week, she started asking what needs to get done without her, which surfaced how few of the decisions still routing through her actually required her involvement. She closes with a warning about talent retention: strong performers can feel when the bench is empty, when every real decision still travels up to the manager, and they quietly start deciding whether the role has a ceiling the manager built by being fast at everything and slow to develop anyone else.
points: Mulder distinguishes responsibility (a task on a job description) from ownership (accountability for the result plus the authority to decide), arguing most managers hand out the former while keeping the latter.
Her diagnostic shift is reframing the weekly planning question from 'what needs to get done' to 'what needs to get done without me,' forcing an honest audit of which decisions actually require her.
Silently fixing a team member's work without telling them what changed feels like protecting quality but actually prevents anyone else from improving, since there's no feedback loop attached.
She warns that strong performers notice an 'empty bench' and quietly calculate whether the team has a ceiling built by the manager's own habit of staying fast rather than developing others.
quotes: For years I redid my team's work. Not all of it. But enough that I'd get something from them, look at it, and think it's faster if I just fix this myself.
Looking back, what I was actually doing was making sure nobody ever got better at it. Nobody learns from work that gets fixed without them ever hearing about it.

There's a big difference between giving someone responsibility and giving someone ownership. Responsibility means they have a task to do, the one written in their job description. Ownership means they're accountable for the result, and with that comes the authority to make decisions they also own.
I stopped asking what needs to get done this week and started asking what needs to get done without me. That sounds like a small shift. But small hinges swing big doors.
Most of the time the answer is no. Most of what was going through me didn't need me. It needed a clear standard, a defined outcome, somebody trained to it, and permission to decide.

They can tell when every real decision travels up. They don't usually say it, but the good ones start calculating whether this is a place they can grow into something bigger, or whether they've already hit the ceiling.
